agents.name: PentestGPT

paper.title: PentestGPT: An LLM Empowered Automatic Penetration Testing
paper.affiliation: Nanyang Technological University / UC Santa Barbara
paper.summary: Single agent + Pentesting Task Tree (PTT) + 3 LLM modules (Reasoning / Generation / Parsing). Modules use independent sessions to prevent context pollution. No role differentiation.

benchmark.dataset: Custom HackTheBox-style machines (13 total) + HackTheBox (10) + picoMini CTF (21)
benchmark.notes: Ablation: removing Reasoning Module drops to 53.6% — PTT is core contribution. GPT-4 vs naive: +58.6%

limitations: Hard difficulty machines: 0/2 solved across all configurations
Single tool output (dirbuster/gobuster) can consume thousands of tokens — no compression mechanism
No multi-host / lateral movement design — single-machine scope only
No role differentiation — single LLM handles all attack phases sequentially
No Memory beyond PTT tree — no cross-session learning

techniques.notes: nmap active scanning is first step in every session
Network service discovery via nmap output parsing
File/directory discovery via dirbuster/gobuster — causes context explosion
Exploit Public-Facing Application — web vulns are primary target
Command execution attempted; harder shells sometimes fail
Software discovery via tool output parsing
System info discovery via shell commands
Privilege escalation attempted but hard machines fail (0/2)
No lateral movement — single-machine design
No multi-C2 or fallback channel

agents.name: Decepticon

paper.title: Decepticon — Autonomous Red Team Agent
paper.venue: GitHub / XBOW benchmark (no formal venue found as of 2026-05-18)
paper.summary: 16 specialized agents orchestrated via LangGraph with engagement discipline (RoE + OPPLAN + MITRE ATT&CK mapping pre-generated). Fresh context per objective prevents noise accumulation. Neo4j stores findings graph. Supports interactive shells via tmux + prompt detection.

benchmark.notes: Highest published score on XBOW Hard as of 2026-05-18. Supports msfconsole, sliver-client, evil-winrm via tmux.

limitations: Fresh context rebuilt per objective: no cross-session or cross-objective knowledge accumulation
Neo4j stores findings graph only — not an attack knowledge graph (no ATT&CK technique nodes or planning)
No Tactic-level reflection: agent cannot reason about 'which ATT&CK stage am I in globally'
12.5% failure cases on XBOW Hard (1/8) — specific failure cause not documented publicly
No formal academic paper — no reproducible benchmark methodology published

agents.name: CAI

paper.title: CAI: An Open, Bug Bounty-Ready Cybersecurity AI
paper.summary: Open-source cybersecurity AI framework. Modular agent architecture with Handoffs (agent routing), Guardrails (prompt injection defense), HITL checkpoints. 300+ model support. Community + Professional (€350/mo, alias1 model) tiers. Validated on OT/ICS CTF, Bug Bounty, robotics, and web security.

benchmark.dataset: Dragos ICS/OT CTF 2025 (34 challenges) + HackTheBox + HackerOne
benchmark.score: 32/34 (94.1%) OT CTF, Rank 1; +37% vs top human teams; alias1 claims to beat GPT-5 on HackTheBox
benchmark.notes: OT/ICS CTF is primary benchmark — Enterprise ATT&CK coverage is secondary; no single published Enterprise number

limitations: No global attack knowledge graph: agent selection is Handoffs-based (dynamic routing), not ATT&CK-driven planning
No persistent memory stream across sessions: standard context window only
Strongest capability (alias1 model) locked behind €350/month Professional tier — Community Edition uses commodity models
OT/ICS primary focus — Enterprise ATT&CK coverage depth unverified in published benchmarks
No formal reproducible benchmark for Enterprise pentest (HackTheBox claim lacks published methodology)

techniques.notes: Active scanning via built-in recon tools
Network service discovery — recon phase
Exploit public-facing app: PortSwigger race condition → web shell; Mercado Libre API enumeration
Credentials in files: Unitree G1 RSA key world-writable; Ecoforest DES weak crypto
File and directory discovery — built-in tools
Command execution via built-in security tools
Network DoS — out of scope for offensive AI framework
Remote services — lateral movement unclear in published case studies
Privilege escalation attempted in some case studies — depth unverified
